course_description:
This course provides an introduction to research in physics. Students choose a topic and a supervisor, and submit a written report by the end of semester. Students commencing in sem 1 enrol in PHYS7743 for sem 1 and sem 2; students commencing in sem 2 enrol in PHYS7744 for sem 2 and the following sem 1. Students completing in single semester enrol in PHYS7745.

Experimental, theoretical or computational project on a topic approved by the Physics Postgraduate Coursework Convenor. The major assessment item is a Masters Thesis submitted after two semesters work described the research and outcomes. There are also two seminars to be presented. Students commencing in Semester 1 enrol in PHYS7743; students commencing in Semester 2 enrol in PHYS7744.

We value and respect the diverse range of experiences our students bring to their education, and we believe that this diversity is crucial for fostering a rich culture of knowledge sharing and meaningful exploration. Our Inclusivity Champions are here to listen, to understand your concerns, and to explore potential actions that can be taken to resolve them. timetable:
Additional timetable information
There is an optional `Research Training' session - 1 hour / week - There is a one hour weekly lecture time scheduled to introduce and discuss the various research milestones as the semesters proceed. A timetable of topics will be released via Blackboard. Note that not all of these lecture times will be devoted to this course, but will be directed at several research courses, including MSc, MQTech, and Honours.
You should have regular meetings as agreed with your supervisor. Typically this is one hour a week.
You need to map out a program of work with your supervisor in the early weeks of your project, as background to your project plan (due end of 2nd week), and discuss updates of the program at regular intervals. Ideally, these conversations will occur prior to semester start.
You are strongly encouraged to take a recreational break during the break between teaching semesters.
course_aims: The aim of the 2 Semester Long Research Project is to develop the research skills of the student by carrying out a small, novel project at the cutting edge of a specialised area of physics.ﾠ It will prepare them for future research careers, or entry into postgraduate study such as an MPhil or PhD research higher degree.

learning_outcomes.description: Be able to plan, develop and carry out an independent research project.
Obtain an in-depth knowledge of the specific topic area through a thorough literature review.
Develop research skills and be able to locate and use information sources.
Present results of research in a written thesis.
Present results of research in an oral seminar.

assessment_details.task_description: Each student will submit a written progress report. Discuss in detail with your supervisor the progress that has been made and what steps are needed to finish the project, as well as an appropriate format for the report. The report should include a comprehensive background and literature review in a form appropriate for inclusion in the thesis. Include the background theory needed for a non-expert to understand your project. The report should also include a description of the progress of the research work to date and a brief plan for the rest of the project. Length is typically 10-15 pages. The style of writing and referencing should be the same as that expected for the thesis. You can write your report in whatever format you like (TeX, Word, etc). Discuss with your supervisor what may be appropriate. A thesis template, which you may find useful, is available. assessment_details.title: Masters Thesis
assessment_details.task_description: At the end of the course, each student will submit a written thesis and subsequently undertake a final talk and oral examination. The thesis is due by 5:00 pm on Monday of the first week of the examination period . The final talk and oral examination must be held after submission of the thesis and before the end of the examination period. The exact date and time should be arranged by the student in consultation with the supervisor, and the two additional examiners: a subject-matter expert and a non-specialist examiner. The thesis should introduce the project and explain its motivation and the broader context of the research field. It should demonstrate familiarity with the relevant literature. The literature review submitted halfway through the year will likely provide the basis for this part of the thesis. The description of the project should be sufficiently detailed to allow a new student to understand how the work was conducted and, where appropriate, reproduce it using the information provided. The thesis must clearly identify which aspects of the project were completed by the student. The research results should be presented clearly and interpreted critically. The student should explain how the findings relate to the current state of research in the area. The conclusion may also discuss possible extensions of the project and directions for future work. The expected length of the thesis is approximately 50 pages. This is a guideline rather than a strict requirement. Heavily theoretical theses may be shorter, whereas experimental theses containing many plots or substantial amounts of data may be longer. Conciseness and clarity are valued by the assessors, and a densely written thesis may communicate the required material in fewer pages. A Physics thesis template is available and may be used in preparing the thesis. Students are strongly encouraged to submit a draft of the thesis to their supervisor or supervisors for feedback well before the submission deadline, normally at least one week before the final talk. Students who believe that they may be unable to submit the thesis by the deadline because of extenuating circumstances should contact both their supervisor or supervisors and the course coordinator as soon as the circumstances become apparent. assessment_details.title: Oral Defense
assessment_details.task_description: During the exam period after you hand in your report you will attend (either in person or online via Zoom or similar video conferencing technology) an oral examination with the examiners and your project supervisor. You will need to discuss a suitable date and venue with your project supervisor, examiners, and course coordinator. The examination will be conducted by a panel of three examiners: the project supervisor; an examiner with expertise relevant to the project; and a non-specialist examiner. The examination will normally last approximately 20–40 minutes. At the beginning of the examination, the student will give a brief presentation of approximately 10 minutes, summarising the project’s motivation, aims, methods, principal results, and conclusions. The remainder of the examination will consist of questions from the panel. Students are expected to demonstrate an understanding of the complete thesis, including material developed collaboratively or with guidance from the supervisor. Questions will not be limited to material covered in the opening presentation. Questions may address: the motivation, aims, and scientific context of the project; the student’s individual contribution to the work; the theoretical, experimental, or computational methods used; the reasons for important methodological or analytical decisions; the interpretation, reliability, and limitations of the results; the relationship between the results and the existing literature; alternative interpretations or approaches; possible improvements, extensions, or future directions; and the communication of the project to both specialist and non-specialist audiences. This assessment item will be audio-visually recorded and retained in accordance with University requirements.
